newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria c.banker optimistic on currency board.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria c.banker optimistic on currency board.

text.p: The head of the Bulgarian National Bank Issue Department, the lynchpin of a currency board system designed to help the economy recover, said on Monday he was confident the arrangement would succeed.

Under an agreement with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) Bulgaria is due to introduce on July 1 a fixed exchange rate mechanism which requires levs in circulation be matched by the BNB foreign exchange reserves.
"We have sufficient cover for our lev liabilities," Martin Zaimov, also a BNB deputy governor, said in an interview with Reuters and Reuters Financial Television.
"I believe that there will be no problems," he added.

"I am rather confident that the banking system will support the fixed exchange rate...the banking system has hardly been ever any stronger," said Zaimov, a 35-year old economist trained at London's Birkbeck College.

A chain of bad loans and lavish lending in the banking sector was halted last year only when the central bank placed a third of the country's banks under supervision and started bankruptcy proceedings against them.
The main mechanism for maintaining liquidity in the banking system will be through interest rates, rising on low liquidity and falling in times of excess liquidity, said Zaimov.
Under Bulgaria's currency board arrangement, the central bank pledges that it will have one German mark for every one thousand levs, freezing the exchange rate at that level.

The gross foreign exchange reserves consisting of gold, foreign currency and foreign securities, amount to 2.7 billion German marks, which are expected to cover BNB liabilities worth 2.2 trillion levs or 2.2 billion marks, said Zaimov.
The liabilities comprise the deposits of banks, deposits of the government, and the levs in circulation.
The Issue Department will publish a weekly balance sheet, with the first one to be released on Tuesday afternoon, said Zaimov.

"The main change is psychological. We have been functioning under a similar system in for around three months. The main difference from the past is that we are now obliged to sell at a fixed exchange rate," said Zaimov.
Delayed reforms and economic mismanagement in the past seven years sent Bulgaria's economy into a tailspin earlier this year.

An IMF agreement in March and ensuing stringent measures introduced by the government helped the lev recover to around 1,700 to the dollar from a 3,000 per dollar nosedive in February and bring down inflation to 5.6 percent in May from 243 percent in February.
